methods.label: Align and subtract the repeating tails
methods.explanation:
Assume the convention used by the choices: \(D=0.PQQQ\ldots\), and juxtaposed blocks such as \(PQ\) mean digit concatenation. Also use \(P\) and \(Q\) for the integer values of their blocks, preserving any leading zeros in their lengths \(r\) and \(s\). Here \(s\ge1\); if \(r=0\), the empty prefix has value \(P=0\).

Let \(T=0.QQQ\ldots\). Multiplication by a power of ten moves the decimal point, so
\[
\begin{aligned}
10^rD&=P+T,\\
10^{r+s}D&=10^sP+Q+T,\\
10^{r+2s}D&=10^{2s}P+10^sQ+Q+T.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are exactly the decimal shifts described in B, C, and E; A is the assumed block representation.

Subtracting the first equation from the second cancels the entire repeating tail:
\[
10^r(10^s-1)D=P(10^s-1)+Q.
\]
Thus the correct right side is \(P(10^s-1)+Q\), rather than \(Q(P-1)\). For example, \(D=0.1\overline2\) gives \(P=1\), \(Q=2\), and \(r=s=1\). The left side in choice D is \(11\), while its proposed right side is \(0\). Under the stated convention, the answer is choice D.

The unrestricted wording has an issue: it only calls \(D\) a repeating decimal. For \(D=1.2\overline3\), with decimal blocks \(P=2\), \(Q=3\), and \(r=s=1\), A is false because \(D\ne0.2\overline3\). Choice D is also false: its left side is \(90D=111\), while its right side is \(3\). Consequently, without a zero-integer-part convention, there need not be just one incorrect expression. Choice D is therefore a conditional answer.
